title: CAN SEXUAL DESIRE ACTUALLY HONOR GOD? PROVERBS 5 GIVES MARRIED DESIRE A SURPRISING PLACE
paragraphs: CAN SEXUAL DESIRE ACTUALLY HONOR GOD? PROVERBS 5 GIVES MARRIED DESIRE A SURPRISING PLACE

What if the desire some Christians learned to feel ashamed of is something Scripture itself celebrates—when it is surrendered to God, protected by covenant, and directed toward the husband or wife He has given you?
There are Bible verses people quote in church.
And then there are Bible verses people quietly hope the pastor never explains while their children are sitting beside them.
Proverbs 5:18–19 belongs to the second category.
Read it slowly.
Not through the embarrassment of modern church culture. Not through pornography. Not through Hollywood. Not through the wounds of your past.
Read it as Scripture.

“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth. Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19 in the King James Version.
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
And perhaps the surprising thing is not that Scripture speaks so openly about married desire.
Perhaps the surprising thing is how many Christians have unknowingly allowed the world to define sexuality more loudly than the God who created it.
The Hebrew is even more striking.
Proverbs 5:18 says:
יְהִֽי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yehi meqorkha barukh, usmach me'eshet ne'urekha.
“May your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
Then comes verse 19:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The thought is powerful: be continually captivated, exhilarated, even intoxicated by her love.
This is not language imported into Scripture by a sexually obsessed culture.
It is sitting there in the Hebrew text of Proverbs.
And suddenly an uncomfortable question becomes unavoidable.
Can sexual desire actually honor God?
Yes—but Scripture's answer is far more beautiful, and far more demanding, than simply saying desire is good.
Because Proverbs 5 is not permission to worship desire.
It is a command to give desire a holy home.
Look at the chapter.

Before Solomon speaks about delighting in one's wife, he warns his son about sexual temptation. What initially tastes like honey eventually becomes bitter. He describes the devastating consequences of adultery and then tells his son to stay far from the door that leads toward it.
Then the imagery changes.
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
And immediately afterward comes the contrast:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
The structure matters.
The Bible is not saying, “Desire doesn't matter.”
It is essentially saying:
Your desire matters so much that you must guard where you take it.
Your sexuality matters so much that it must not be scattered among strangers.
Your spouse matters so much that faithfulness should be more than merely refusing adultery.
There should also be delight.

The contrast in Proverbs 5:15–21 is unmistakable: one's own cistern, one's own well, one's own covenant relationship—rather than the forbidden embrace outside it. Multiple English translations preserve the unusually strong language of satisfaction, delight, captivation, exhilaration, or intoxication within that marital context.
That changes something.
Because some people grew up believing holiness meant becoming almost embarrassed by the fact that they possessed sexual desire at all.
So they entered marriage carrying shame into a place God intended for covenant intimacy.
Others went in the opposite direction.
They were taught by pornography, casual relationships, fantasies, affairs, entertainment, social media, and a culture of endless comparison that desire should never be denied anything.
One message says:
“Your desire is dirty.”
The other says:
“Your desire is your master.”
Scripture bows to neither.
God says your desire needs redemption.
That distinction is enormous.
Sexual desire was never meant to sit on the throne.
Jesus belongs there.
But when Christ is Lord, human desires can be reordered beneath His authority.
And within biblical marriage, sexual intimacy does not have to be treated as an embarrassing concession to human weakness.
It can become part of covenant delight.
Part of tenderness.
Part of exclusivity.
Part of knowing and being known.
Part of two people repeatedly saying with their bodies what their vows already declared with their mouths:
I choose you.
Still you.
Only you.
This is why Proverbs 5 is simultaneously sensual and severe.
The same chapter that celebrates a husband's delight in his wife warns that sin eventually becomes a rope.
“His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself, and he shall be holden with the cords of his sins.”
Proverbs 5:22.
That is frighteningly accurate to the nature of habitual sexual sin.
At first, you hold it.
Eventually, it holds you.
At first, you visit the fantasy.
Eventually, the fantasy follows you home.
At first, it is only a message.
Only a look.
Only a private search.
Only a conversation your spouse doesn't know about.
Only one more video.
Only one more secret.
Only one more compromise.
Until one day you realize the thing you insisted you controlled has begun controlling you.
Scripture describes sin as cords.
And cords are rarely frightening when they are still individual threads.
That may be where someone reading this needs to stop pretending.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your family doesn't know.
Your church doesn't know.
Your friends would never suspect it.
Your browser history tells one story.
Your public Christianity tells another.
You know exactly when to close the screen.
You know exactly what to delete.
You know exactly how to smile afterward.
But Proverbs 5:21 quietly walks into the room:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings.”
God sees.
Not merely the scandal if it becomes public.
He sees the road toward it.
And that sentence can feel terrifying until you remember who the Gospel reveals God to be.
The God who sees is also the God who calls sinners home.
This is where Christianity is radically different from merely telling sexually broken people to behave better.
The Gospel does not begin with pretending your history never happened.
It begins with Jesus Christ entering the story you cannot rewrite yourself.
Maybe your story includes pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe years of lust.
Maybe emotional infidelity.
Maybe promiscuity.
Maybe secret messages.
Maybe fantasies you have fed for so long that you no longer remember what freedom felt like.

Maybe you are married and the passion that once seemed effortless has been buried underneath children, exhaustion, arguments, disappointment, aging, rejection, resentment, illness, schedules, bills, and years of things neither of you ever properly said.
Maybe the problem isn't forbidden desire.
Maybe you barely desire each other anymore.

And perhaps reading Proverbs 5 hurts because “rejoice with the wife of thy youth” sounds beautiful until you remember that you and your spouse hardly recognize the people you were when you first made those vows.
Listen carefully.
Proverbs 5 is wisdom, not a weapon.

It should never be used to pressure a spouse into sexual activity, excuse selfishness, ignore consent, minimize pain, or demand intimacy while refusing tenderness, faithfulness, patience, repentance, and love.
Biblical marital intimacy is not permission to use another person's body.
Covenant love is not consumption.
Your husband is not a machine built to satisfy you.
Your wife is not an object God handed you.
They bear God's image.
And Christian marriage ultimately belongs underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
This is why the deepest question is not merely:
“What am I allowed to desire?”
It is:
“Does Jesus rule what I desire?”
Because Christ does not merely want access to the religious section of your life.
He wants the locked rooms too.
The browser.
The fantasy.
The resentment.
The marriage bed.
The loneliness.
The memories.
The wounds.
The hunger for validation.
The secret attraction.
The private messages.
The part of you that desperately wants to be wanted.
The part of you that is ashamed of wanting anything at all.
All of it.
And this is where grace becomes almost scandalous.
Jesus does not wait for sexually broken people to become spotless before calling them toward Himself.
He calls sinners to repent.
Repentance does not mean pretending the sin was harmless.
It means agreeing with God about it and turning toward Him.
Grace does not rename bondage as freedom.
Grace breaks the chains and teaches the captive how to walk again.
Forgiveness is not God saying your sin did not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we wanted to admit.
Forgiveness is God saying Christ's blood is sufficient for repentant sinners who come to Him.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe your sexuality has been tangled with shame for decades.
Maybe you learned desire from pornography before anyone taught you covenant.
Maybe nobody ever told you that God designed sexual faithfulness not merely as a list of prohibitions but as protection for something precious.
You cannot travel backward.
You cannot become the person who never clicked it.
Never watched it.
Never sent it.
Never touched.
Never cheated.
Never lied.
Never crossed the boundary.
Never shattered the trust.
But Jesus Christ is not limited to editing your past.
He redeems people.
And redeemed people can begin walking differently today.
That may mean confession.
That may mean ending the secret relationship.
That may mean deleting the hidden account.
That may mean getting serious pastoral counsel and professional help for entrenched patterns.
That may mean rebuilding trust slowly instead of demanding immediate forgiveness from the person you wounded.
That may mean learning to pursue your spouse again without entitlement.
That may mean having an awkward conversation tonight instead of living another silent year.
That may mean telling Jesus the truth you have been disguising with religious language.
And for some reading this, the first honest prayer may contain only four words:
Jesus, have mercy on me.
That is enough honesty to begin.
And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual sin or restored something you thought was permanently destroyed, perhaps your comment needs to become somebody else's reason not to give up:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading underneath you may desperately need that testimony.
Because the world already knows how to make sex scandalous.
Jesus knows how to take scandal and lead sinners toward grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that celebrates adultery.
Not grace that baptizes lust.
Not grace that tells us holiness no longer matters.
Transforming grace.
Grace that teaches wandering eyes to come home.
Grace that teaches wounded spouses how to pursue healing wisely.
Grace that teaches desire that it has a Master.
Grace that takes what sin distorted and brings it back beneath the authority of Christ.
And perhaps that is the great surprise hiding inside Proverbs 5.
God is not anti-desire.
He is against the destruction caused when desire rebels against its Creator.

Within the covenant of marriage, Scripture can speak positively and remarkably openly about delight between husband and wife. Outside covenant faithfulness, that same chapter warns of consequences, captivity, and ruin.
God's answer to destructive desire is therefore not merely suppression.
It is sanctification.
Desire surrendered.
Desire disciplined.
Desire faithful.
Desire that refuses to turn another human being into an object.
Desire that learns the difference between consuming someone and loving someone.
Desire that can look at a spouse after years of ordinary mornings, arguments, wrinkles, responsibilities, disappointments, forgiveness, laughter, children, grief, and survival and still whisper:
I choose you.
There is something profoundly holy about that.
Not because sexual desire itself saves anybody.
It doesn't.
Jesus saves.
Not because marriage makes anyone righteous.
It doesn't.
Christ's righteousness is our hope.

But because when every part of human life is brought beneath the lordship of Jesus, even desires that sin has grotesquely distorted can be reordered toward faithfulness, gratitude, tenderness, and covenant love.
So husbands and wives...
Do not let pornography teach you how to see the person you promised to love.
Do not let algorithms convince you that someone else's body is more deserving of your attention than the person whose heart you vowed to protect.
Do not let familiarity become contempt.
Do not let resentment quietly murder tenderness.
Do not outsource to strangers what belongs inside your covenant.
Talk.
Repent.
Forgive wisely.
Seek help when needed.
Flirt again.
Laugh again.
Pray together.
Hold hands when nobody is watching.
Pursue one another without coercion.
Protect the covenant before you have to rescue it from catastrophe.
And remember that the God who commands faithfulness is also the God who created delight.
There may come a night when temptation is louder than wisdom, and you will need to remember that God is not merely calling you away from something destructive.
He is calling you toward something holy.
Send this privately to the believer who thinks one sexual failure has disqualified them forever.
It cannot.
It does not.
And not because Christians should ever be manipulated into giving.
Paul's language in 2 Corinthians 9:7 is explicit:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Give as one has purposed in the heart—not “under compulsion.”
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Christian generosity is meant to rise from a willing heart, not spiritual pressure.
A share can still carry Scripture into a home we could never enter.
A comment can tell a struggling believer they are not fighting alone.
A tag can place truth in front of someone at precisely the moment they need it.
A saved article can become tomorrow night's reminder when temptation returns.
And a life surrendered to Jesus can become something infinitely greater than engagement statistics could ever measure.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question that no algorithm can answer for you:
What part of my desire have I still refused to surrender to Jesus?
Do not answer quickly.
Let it become prayer.
Because perhaps the real scandal was never that the Bible speaks openly about desire.
Perhaps the scandal is that Christ knows everything we have desired wrongly...
everything we have hidden...
every boundary we crossed...
every person we wounded...
every promise we broke...
and still calls sinners out of darkness, toward repentance, into grace, and onward into transformation.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have authority to become your savior.
Your desires may speak loudly.
They do not get to become your lord.
Your sin may have written pages you would give anything to erase.
But the pen is not ultimately in sin's hand.
Bring Jesus the chapter you are most ashamed to let anyone read—because grace is still writing where you thought the story had already ended.
